title: Ox and self forgotten
hookLine: eighth picture: both ox and self forgotten, an empty circle
carry: let go of the seeker too

cards: Turn to the eighth picture and there's nothing on it. No herdsman, no ox, no hut, no field, no rope. Just a circle drawn in ink, with empty paper inside.
For seven pictures you've followed a man and an animal through grass and mud and weather. Yesterday the ox dropped out of the frame and the man stayed. Now he's gone too.
It can look as if a page went missing at the printer. It didn't.

teach.b: First, both forgotten. The Chinese title says it directly: person and ox, both forgotten. The verse, in paraphrase, lists them as they go: whip, rope, person, ox, all gone into emptiness.
Yesterday he let go of what he was chasing. Today he lets go of himself as the one who chased it.
Second, no place to stand. The preface says he doesn't linger where there is awakening, and passes quickly by where there is none. It isn't that he vanished.
There's just no fixed spot left to point at and say, there he is, the enlightened man.
Third, no praise can reach it. The preface mentions birds bringing flowers, an old story of a hermit so holy that birds brought him offerings, and says that praise would mean nothing here.
The verse adds: the sky is too vast for anyone to survey; a snowflake can't fall on a blazing furnace. Even the idea of being special melts.
An empty frame could look like loss, but a circle is unbroken. In Japanese Zen, drawing a circle in one brushstroke, the enso, became its own practice, showing the mind at the moment of the stroke.
The emptiness here isn't a blank where something used to be. It's the paper the whole story was drawn on, still here when the herdsman and the ox are gone.

how: In Zen, the eighth oxherding picture is drawn as an empty circle, and in Japanese Zen the enso, a circle brushed in one stroke, is practiced and hung in temples and homes as an expression of the mind at that moment.

o: self and ox both let go, shown as one unbroken circle
a sign that the herdsman gave up and went away
a blank page where a picture was lost at the printer

games.q: the empty circle: tap the pairs.
p: the ox gone, the man remains
a circle brushed in one stroke

s: the eighth picture was lost, so the page is blank
the empty circle is the picture: person and ox both forgotten.
the preface says he doesn't settle in awakening or in its absence
that's why there's no fixed spot to point at.
the empty circle means everything was lost
a circle is whole; the story happened inside it, and it remains.

games.q: you're painting the eighth picture. the herdsman and ox are both forgotten. what do you put on the page?
o: the herdsman meditating, with a halo.
a single circle with nothing inside.
the ox standing alone in the field.
games.why: the eighth picture is an empty circle. no enlightened figure, because there's no fixed self left to show.

practice: If there's paper and a pen nearby, draw a circle once, in one movement; if not, trace one slowly in the air with a finger. Don't fix it: wobbly is fine, it's yours.
Then look at the inside, empty and missing nothing, and let breath and thoughts come and go inside it.

wordCard.voice: The empty circle. The eighth oxherding picture: ox and self both forgotten, a single circle with nothing inside, whole and unbroken. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (renniu juwang): 'person and ox both forgotten', the name of the eighth oxherding picture.

carryVoice: Your line: let go of the seeker too. Ox and self forgotten, nothing missing, and no one left keeping score. See you on the other side of the circle.
